title: The dark night, again
hook: John of the Cross: God works in darkness, weaning us from feelings

segments.voice: Yesterday, a saint's long darkness: Mother Teresa's letters, and a woman who kept going without feeling God near. Your line was faith without feeling. What faithful thing did you do anyway? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

A tiny cell. Almost no light. Tradition says a Spanish friar named John was locked in a room like this by members of his own religious order, who didn't like his reforms. No books. Bread and water. And in that darkness, tradition says, he began to compose poems in his head. Out of that time, the story goes, came a poem that begins on a dark night, with a soul slipping out of a quiet house, unseen, guided by no light except the one burning in the heart. We met this phrase earlier on the path. Today we go back with a sharper question: what is the darkness for? Today: the dark night.

John of the Cross later wrote a long explanation of his poem, and the picture at its center is a mother and a child. At first, he says, God treats a new believer like a mother nursing a baby: warm, sweet, easy. Prayer feels good. Church feels good. Then, like any mother, God begins to wean the child. The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so the child can grow up and eat real food. The Psalms already use this image: "my soul is even as a weaned child." And Paul tells the Corinthians, "I have fed you with milk, and not with meat." Second, what the weaning is aimed at. John says that a soul can come to love the good feelings of prayer more than God. So God gently removes the feelings. What's left, in his telling, if you stay, is a love that doesn't depend on getting something back. That's the night working. Third, how to tell it apart. John was careful. He wrote that not every dryness is this night; some comes from sin, carelessness or sickness of body and mind, and he told guides to tell them apart. That's worth holding next to a lesson from a few days ago: depression needs care and help, and naming something a dark night is no reason to skip it. Last, what to do inside it. John's advice is surprisingly simple: don't strain to force the old feelings back. Stay quiet, with a loving attention, and let God work. The psalm says, "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." In the psalm, the night isn't empty to God. For John, night is working.

Here's the practice: trust in the dark. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes, and let the darkness behind your eyelids be just what it is. Don't try to make anything happen, no special feeling, no picture, no answer. Just stay, with a quiet, open attention, the way you'd sit in a dark room waiting for your eyes to adjust. If you pray, you can simply rest there before God, without words. If you don't, rest in the not-knowing. The bell holds the time.
The dark night. John of the Cross's name for the season when God takes away the sweetness of prayer, the way a mother weans a child, so love can grow up.
Your line: night is working. Today, when something feels flat or dry, stay with it for one more minute before reaching for a distraction. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and Doctor of the Church, and his poem and commentary are read by Christians of several churches; spiritual directors draw on his advice to help people tell a season of dryness in prayer apart from depression or neglect.

fork.setup: you've prayed for years, and suddenly it feels like nothing. no warmth, no words. what does John of the Cross advise?
options: try harder to make the feelings come back.
stay quiet before God, with a loving attention, and let it work.
stop praying until the feeling returns.
fork.reveal: John says not to strain after the old sweetness. stay quiet and attentive: in his telling, the night itself is doing the work.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dark night of the soul means a very bad time.
what it means: for John of the Cross, a season when God takes away the sweetness of prayer, like a mother weaning a child, so love can grow up.
what a scholar hears: John wrote the poem and then long commentaries on it, and he carefully separates this night from dryness caused by sin, carelessness or sickness.

notes: John's imprisonment (a tiny cell, by members of his own order, over his reforms, bread and water, composing poems in his head) is given as 'tradition says'; confirm details.

The poem and commentary are paraphrased, not quoted: the opening image (a soul slipping out of a quiet house, guided only by the light in the heart), the weaning image (Book I, ch. 1), loving the sweetness of prayer more than God, the signs distinguishing the night from dryness caused by sin, carelessness or bodily/mental illness (Book I, ch. 9), and the advice to stay in loving attention (Book I, ch. 10). Confirm chapter references and fairness.
Original-language game left null: John wrote in Spanish (noche oscura), which the validator flags as plain ASCII; a Keeper may add it.
Day title says 'again': assumes an earlier lesson on the path introduced the dark night ('We met this phrase earlier on the path'). Confirm.
Link back to day 1383 (depression needs care) is deliberate; confirm tone.

Editor pass: cut the uncited cell measurement ('barely wider than a man lying down') and 'because he had nothing to write with'; the hook no longer says the Dark Night poem itself was composed in the cell (accounts usually place its writing after his escape), only that it came 'out of that time'.
Audit: two lines read as the narrator's own claims about God ("To God, the night isn't empty"; what is left "if you stay"); now attributed to the psalm and to John.
